connector: Marilla Cuthbert. I’ve finished three new dresses for the child, good plain ones, and I’ll show them to her presently. She starts Sunday school this week as well, so there’s plenty to get right. I expect she’ll have something to say about the dresses. She generally has something to say. Come along and see whether she’s grateful.

a.raw: anne sat on the bed looking sadly at the plain sleeves
a.fixed: Anne sat on the bed, looking sadly at the plain sleeves.
a.why: A capital letter on the name Anne, a comma before the describing phrase that tells what she was doing, and a period at the end.

b.raw: marilla stood in the doorway waiting for a word of thanks
b.fixed: Marilla stood in the doorway, waiting for a word of thanks.
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on the name Marilla, a comma before the describing phrase that tells what she was doing, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what Marilla thought she was giving Anne, and what Anne thought she was being given.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what the flowers cost Anne, and whether she knew it when she picked them.
scholar.journal-q3: … and point to one detail from the class that shows the sleeves were never really about sleeves.

fill1.h1: To miss something is to let your eyes pass above it. Which part means above or across?
fill1.why: over- means above or across: to overlook is to look right across something and miss it.

fill2.h1: This coat goes on top of the others. Which part means above?
fill2.why: over- means above: an overcoat goes over your other clothes.

fill3.h1: A ship that goes beneath the sea. Which of the two review parts is the short one that means under?
fill3.why: sub- means under: a submarine travels under the sea.

fill4.h1: Below the surface. This one is the plain English word for beneath.
fill4.why: under- means below: underground is below the ground.

match.solemn: Solemn is about how serious a moment is, with no joking in it. Look for the meaning about being serious.
match.resolute: Resolute has resolve inside it, the feeling of having made up your mind. Look for the meaning about being firm.
match.enraptured: Enraptured has rapt inside it, carried away. Look for the meaning about great joy.
match.vindictive: Vindictive is about wanting to pay somebody back. Look for the meaning about revenge.

sort.puffed sleeves: You could touch these, and Anne certainly wanted to. Which column holds things your senses can meet?
sort.hat: A hat is a real object you could hold in your hand. Which column holds things like that?
sort.imagination: You cannot photograph an imagination, only what it makes. Which column holds ideas and feelings?
sort.despair: Despair is a feeling. Real, but not touchable. Which column holds feelings and ideas?
sort.class: A class is one word for a whole group of children acting together. Which column holds words like that?
sort.congregation: A congregation is many people named as one group. Which column holds words for groups?
sort.a·bout: Say it lazily: uh-BOUT. Which letter is spelling that first mumbled sound?
sort.a·go: Say it lazily: uh-GO. Look at the letter in the unstressed first syllable.
sort.les·son: Say it: LESS-un. The second syllable is mumbled. Which letter is sitting there?
sort.rib·bon: Say it: RIB-un. Look at the letter in the second syllable, not the sound.
sort.gar·den: Say it: GAR-dun. The mumbled vowel is in the second syllable. Which letter spells it?
sort.mo·ment: Say it: MO-munt. The second syllable is unstressed. Look at its vowel letter.

transcripts.welcome: Marilla Cuthbert here, guiding you again. Today’s question is about wanting something and being told no. You’re to watch how the author shows the wanting and the disappointment in the very same breath. Keep hold of one thing you want yourself that somebody has called foolish. It’ll help you understand her. In word study there’s a new word part, the one that means above, or too much.
transcripts.wgrd: Here’s how to go about it. Before you open the book, settle what you’re looking for: one thing the child decides to do, even a small one. When you find it, don’t move on. Back up a line or two and find what happened just before. That’s your cause. Then read a little past it and see who has to deal with what she did. Hold all three in your head together.
transcripts.dol: Tap the coloured parts of the model before you touch the second sentence, and read what each one tells you. The one you’re fixing starts with a person, and a person’s name starts with a capital letter. Then it tells you where she is, and after that what she was doing. Look at what the model puts between those two parts. Write yours in your notebook, check it against the model, then tap the button.
transcripts.guide1: Word study, and there’s a new word part this week. It means above, or across, or too much, and I dare say you’ll meet it more often than you’d like. Work through the four boxes in order. In each one, read the whole thing before you start tapping and typing. Most mistakes I’ve seen come from starting before you’ve looked. Check as you go, not at the end.
transcripts.morphology: Read the four words at the top and press the button to see them cracked open. Then, in the game, cover the front of each word with your finger and read what’s left. Read the little description after it, too. That description is your clue: does it point above something, or beneath it? Type the part that fits. If you miss one, read the line that comes up before you try again.
transcripts.vocabulary: Do the example at the top first, all three steps, even though the answer’s printed. That’s practice. Then for each of the three cards, read the book’s sentence, guess out loud, and only then tap. In the match at the bottom, do the words you’re sure of first and leave the hardest for last, when there’s only one meaning left. If you match wrong, a line comes up. Read it.
transcripts.grammar: Three columns and nobody’s told you what they are. Good. Move the two words you’re surest about first, one to each side, and ask yourself what makes them different. Then find each one’s partner. The pair left over belong together for a reason of their own, so say what that reason is before you drop them. Then name all three groups in the box, and say how you told them apart.
transcripts.spelling: Say each word out loud before you drag it, and say it the lazy way you would in a hurry. One syllable goes mushy. Find that syllable, then look at which vowel letter is sitting in it. That letter tells you the column, not the sound, because the sound is the same in all six. If you get one wrong, a line will tell you why. Read it before you try again.
transcripts.copia: Here’s a plain sentence from before she’d said a word about the dresses. Say it three ways. First, put something at the front, a where or a when. Second, swap the marked verb for one that shows how she looked, since a person can look at a thing a dozen different ways. Third, tell us more about where or how. Keep it true to the picture. Change one thing at a time.
transcripts.guide2: The child starts Sunday school this week, and she’ll meet other children there, which she’s had little enough of. This week’s watch is friendship. I’ve never had a great deal of use for it myself, but I’ll say this: a friend is somebody you choose, and who chooses you back. As you read, notice whether she has anybody like that yet, and what it costs her that she hasn’t.
transcripts.read: Two stops, and the first comes before she’s even left the house, so look for it early. It asks why a child would care so much about a thing I’ve called ridiculous. Don’t answer for me. Answer for her. The second stop is at the very end, and it’s about honesty. Ask yourself whether saying the true thing is brave or only careless, and have a reason ready either way.
transcripts.guide3: Well. She went to Sunday school alone, since I had a headache coming on, and came home and told me it was horrid. Mr. Bell’s prayer was too long, Miss Rogerson asked a great many questions, and every other girl in the class had puffed sleeves. I ought to have scolded her. The trouble is, some of what she said I’ve thought myself for years. Your turn. Say what you noticed, and show me where.
transcripts.chapter: The first question is about the dresses I made. Look at what she said when she first saw them, and at what she didn’t say. For the second, something happened on the road to church that nobody has told me about yet, so you’ll have to find it yourself. It’s small. Read slowly. The third quotes her exactly. Before you answer, count how many girls in that class had what she didn’t.
transcripts.wordconn: Your morphology answer is saved, so let’s tie it up. This week’s new word part means above, or too much. Well, that child does everything too much, if you ask me. Too much imagination, too much feeling, too much talk. And yet I keep listening. Look back at the sentence you wrote. Does your word say something true about her world? If it doesn’t quite, you’ll know what to reach for next time.
transcripts.workshop: Today you name a want and a wall. Make them small and real. That child wanted puffed sleeves, and I was the wall, and I had my reasons. Notice it wasn’t a grand want. It was sleeves. Then look at what the want tells you about the person: she wanted to look like the other girls. Pick your character’s want the same way. Something you could point at, that shows who they are underneath.
